threads.thread_goal: Align on service scope, target SMEs, and overall value proposition.

messages.text: Kicking off the new SME advisory initiative for project_title: Launch of Data-Driven SME Advisory Service. I have started outlining the service concept in A1 and mapping it to T1, but I would like us to align on scope and target segments before I lock anything in. Right now I am thinking of focusing on established SMEs with at least basic financial statements available, and positioning the service around financial health checks plus simple BI insights. I am not fully sure how far we should go into operational consulting or HR topics in this first version. Can you all share views on which SME profiles we should prioritise and what value statements feel strongest for launch

Thanks for starting this. From a positioning angle, I would keep the first wave very focused: SMEs that already have digital bookkeeping and at least a year of consistent data. That will make it easier to tell a clear story in the market. For value statements in A1, I suggest we anchor on three promises: clarity on financial health, simple forward-looking scenarios, and practical next steps that owners can act on quickly. Anything that sounds like deep restructuring or HR transformation can be framed as a later add-on. For T1, can you add a section that lists what the service does not cover in phase one so we avoid scope creep

From the BI side, I agree with focusing on SMEs that already have structured data. For the scope in A1, I would propose that the core service includes: a standard financial and KPI snapshot, a simple trend analysis over 12 to 24 months, and 3 to 5 key insights translated into business language. Anything more advanced, like predictive models or custom dashboards, could be a later tier. This will also keep T7 manageable when we define the operational playbook. One question: do we want to include any light benchmarking against peers in the first launch, or keep it internal to the client data only

On the financial side, I would suggest we require at least a basic set of statements: profit and loss, balance sheet, and cash flow for the last year. That will make it easier later when we work on T2 and the checklist. For the scope in A1, maybe we should say that we provide structured analysis and general guidance, but not detailed tax planning or legal advice. I am not entirely sure how far we can go in terms of specific recommendations without triggering regulatory issues, so I would like legal to review that part once we have a draft

For external perception, we should keep the promise very concrete and avoid anything that could be interpreted as guaranteed outcomes. In A1, I recommend we describe the service as helping SME owners understand their numbers and make more informed decisions, rather than promising specific profit increases. That will also make it easier later when we build A5 and the PR plan. On target segments, I support the idea of focusing on SMEs with at least one year of digital records and a clear owner-manager, as that gives us a clear persona for messaging

On benchmarking, my first thought was to include some comparison to industry averages, but I am not sure how reliable that would be with our current tools. Maybe we could mention it as a possible future enhancement in A1, and for now keep the core service focused on the clients own data. That might also simplify T7 because consultants would not need to explain complex benchmarks. Does that sound reasonable, or are we missing a strong benefit by not including benchmarks at launch

I would keep benchmarking out of the first launch. With the 30 day timeline and the constraint to use only existing BI tools, we would risk overcomplicating T3 and T9 later. We can still position the insights as tailored to the clients own trends, which is already valuable. I suggest we explicitly state in A1 that phase one focuses on internal performance analysis, and that external benchmarks are on the roadmap. That will keep expectations clear for both clients and consultants

Agree with keeping benchmarks out for now. From a messaging standpoint, it is easier to explain a focused offer than a half-baked comparison feature. We can still use phrases like helping you see how your business is evolving over time. For A1, I will later mirror the agreed scope into the early draft of A5 so that T5 and T10 stay aligned. Could you, in T1, add a short section that lists the main use cases we want to highlight, for example cash flow visibility, profitability by product line, and early warning on risk

I can add those use cases to T1, though I might need some help framing them clearly. So far I have listed general financial health checks and basic performance review. I will expand that to include cash flow visibility and simple profitability views, and I will flag any wording I am unsure about so you can refine it when you work on A5. For the scope in A1, I will also add a section that clarifies we are not providing tax or legal advice, as suggested earlier

One more point on the target SMEs: to make the financial analysis meaningful, we should probably exclude very early stage businesses with no stable revenue yet. Maybe in A1 we can say that the service is designed for SMEs with at least 12 months of trading history. That will also help when we later define minimum data requirements in A2 and A4. I will keep that in mind when drafting T2 and T8, so that the checklists and guidelines match the agreed scope

On use cases, I would prioritise those that translate easily into media stories later: for example, helping owners anticipate cash crunches, understand which products are really profitable, and see the impact of simple decisions like changing payment terms. If we bake those into A1 and T1 now, it will be straightforward to build narratives in A5 and the PR plan. Also, for clarity, I suggest we explicitly state that the first launch focuses on financial and BI insights, and that broader strategic or HR advisory can be referred to partner services if needed

Agree on excluding very early stage businesses for now. From a data perspective, without at least a year of history, the trends and KPIs we can show are limited. I will reflect this in the assumptions when we work on T3 and T9, so that the dashboards and pilot selection criteria match the scope in A1. This will also help us avoid data quality surprises during the pilot

To summarise what I am hearing so far, the core service in A1 would be: for SMEs with at least 12 months of digital financial records, we provide a structured financial and KPI review, simple trend analysis, and a short list of practical recommendations. We explicitly exclude tax, legal, and deep restructuring work from phase one, and we keep external benchmarking as a future enhancement. If that sounds right, we can treat that as the baseline scope for T1 and T7, and I will use it as the foundation for the first messaging draft in A5

That summary matches my understanding. Unless anyone objects, I will update A1 and T1 accordingly and mark this as our initial scope and target segment definition. We can still refine details as we work through the other threads, but this should give us enough clarity to move forward on the playbook in T7 and the pricing work in T4

No objections from my side. For clarity, I suggest we also capture in A1 which use cases are in for the first launch and which we explicitly park for later phases. Based on the discussion, I would say phase one includes: financial health review, cash flow visibility, simple profitability views, and early warning signals. More advanced scenario modelling, external benchmarking, and broader strategic advisory can be listed as future extensions. That will help us manage expectations with both clients and internal teams

Agree with that split between phase one and later phases. I will make sure that when we design the dashboards under T3, we focus only on the phase one use cases you listed. That will keep the BI work aligned with A1 and avoid overbuilding for the pilot. Once we have pilot feedback, we can revisit the roadmap items like benchmarking and more advanced scenarios

I am aligned as well. When I draft T2 and T8, I will treat those phase one use cases as the baseline and make sure the financial checklist and data protection guidelines in A2 and A4 support them. For example, I will include specific items around cash flow data and basic profitability breakdowns, but I will not add complex requirements that belong to later phases

Given the confirmations above, I will proceed on the assumption that D1 and D2 are agreed: the initial scope and target SME segments in A1 are approved, and we have a clear list of phase one use cases versus later enhancements. I will reflect this in the first draft of A5 and in the internal enablement outline for T10 so that sales and support get a consistent story

threads.thread_goal: Agree on the financial and BI assessment framework and data requirements.

messages.text: I have put together a first draft of the Standard SME Financial and BI Assessment Checklist in A2, based on the scope we agreed in A1 and the work planned in T2. The checklist currently covers required financial statements, a basic set of KPIs, and some risk indicators. I am less confident about the BI-related items and the data quality thresholds, and I also want to make sure we align with data protection expectations in A4 and T8. Could you review and suggest what we should add or simplify, especially around minimum data requirements and how strict we should be before accepting a client into the service

Thanks for sharing A2. From a BI perspective, I would suggest we structure the checklist into three parts: data sources, data completeness, and data quality. For minimum requirements, I propose we require at least 12 months of monthly data for revenue, costs, and cash movements, with no more than one missing month. For quality, we can define simple checks like totals matching between statements and no negative revenue values. These criteria can be documented in A2 and mirrored in A4 so that consultants know when to pause and ask for corrections before proceeding. This will also help us later when we design dashboards under T3

Looking at A2 from the consultant side, the checklist feels quite detailed already. I worry a bit that if we make the data requirements too strict, we might turn away SMEs that could still benefit from a lighter review. Would it make sense to have a minimum set of must-have items and then a nice-to-have section, so that in T7 we can define what the consultant does if some data is missing For example, maybe we can still run a partial assessment if cash flow data is incomplete, but we clearly state the limitations in the client report

From a reputation and risk angle, I would lean towards being clear and firm on minimum data standards. If we deliver insights based on weak or incomplete data, it could undermine trust in the service. However, I like the idea of a must-have versus nice-to-have split in A2, as long as we also define in A4 how consultants should communicate any limitations to clients. That way, we protect the brand while still being pragmatic. Once we sign off on A2 and the data criteria, I will reflect the key points in A5 and the PR Q and A so that we do not overpromise

I have gone through A2 as well. For the sake of clarity in sales and marketing materials later, I suggest we keep the client-facing description of requirements simple: for example, digital records for the last 12 months and basic breakdowns of revenue and costs. The more technical criteria, like specific KPIs and data checks, can stay in A2 and A4 for internal use. When we build A8 and T10, we can translate the checklist into a short readiness section that sales can use to qualify prospects without going into accounting jargon

The three-part structure you suggest makes sense. I can rework A2 so that we clearly separate data sources, completeness, and quality checks. I will also add the 12 month requirement and the rule about no more than one missing month. I am not entirely sure how to phrase the negative revenue check and similar items in a way that consultants can easily follow, so I might need your help to review that part once I update the draft

Happy to help refine the wording. We can keep the checks very concrete, for example: confirm that total revenue is non negative for each month, confirm that total assets equal total liabilities plus equity, and confirm that cash opening plus net cash flow equals cash closing. If we list these as simple yes or no items in A2, consultants can follow them without needing deep technical knowledge. I will also make sure that the dashboards we design under T3 highlight any obvious inconsistencies so that issues are visible during the assessment

The must-have versus nice-to-have split would really help in practice. In T7, we can then define two paths: a full assessment when all must-have items in A2 are present, and a limited assessment when some items are missing but the basics are there. For the limited path, we can include a standard disclaimer in the client report template so that expectations are managed. I will need guidance from you and from legal on the exact wording, but at least the structure can be captured in the playbook

That approach works for me, as long as the disclaimer is clear and consistent with A4. We should avoid any language that suggests we are giving guarantees based on partial data. Once A2 and A4 are stable, I will draft a short standard phrase that can be reused in client reports and in any media interactions if questions arise about data limitations. This will also be reflected in the Q and A under T6 so that spokespeople are prepared

Understood on being firm with minimum standards. I will adjust A2 so that the must-have section includes: full set of basic financial statements for the last 12 months, digital format, and no more than one missing month of data. The nice-to-have section can include more detailed breakdowns, like revenue by product or customer segment. I will also cross reference A4 and T8 to ensure that any data handling instructions are consistent with our internal policies. Once I have updated the draft, I will share it again for a quick check before we sign off for the pilot

For the pilot, I suggest we treat the updated A2 as the standard and only make exceptions if we explicitly log them in A7. That way, when we later work on T9 and T12, we can see how data quality affected the insights and client satisfaction. It will also give us evidence to refine the minimum criteria if needed. From my side, once you incorporate the changes, I am comfortable using A2 as the basis for the pilot assessments

On the client acceptance criteria, it might help if we summarise the minimum data requirements into a short checklist that sales can use during early conversations. Once A2 is final, I can extract a simplified version for A8 and T10, focusing on the must-have items only. That will reduce back and forth later when a prospect is interested but does not yet meet the standards. We can then decide whether to help them get ready or to schedule the service for a later date

I like the idea of logging any exceptions in A7 during the pilot. It will give us concrete examples to use in internal communications and, if needed, in refining our external messaging. Once we have a few cases, we can decide whether to tighten or relax certain criteria. For now, I am comfortable stating internally that clients must meet the A2 minimums to be accepted into the service, with any deviations explicitly documented

Given the feedback, I will finalise A2 with the structure and criteria we discussed and treat it as the standard for the pilot. Unless there are strong objections, I suggest we consider the checklist signed off for pilot use once I circulate the updated version later today. For the minimum data quality and completeness criteria, I will document the 12 month requirement, the missing month rule, and the basic consistency checks as the baseline for accepting a client into the service

From my side, I am aligned with treating the updated A2 as signed off for the pilot and using the documented criteria as the gate for client acceptance. I will adjust the BI work under T3 and the pilot planning under T9 to reflect these standards. During the pilot, we can monitor how often clients fail to meet the criteria and whether we need to adjust them before scaling

I will take D3 and D4 as confirmed and start drafting the readiness section for A8 and the internal enablement under T10 based on the A2 minimums. That way, by the time we launch, sales and support will know exactly which clients are a good fit and what data they need to collect upfront

threads.thread_goal: Finalize pricing, packaging, and commercial positioning for launch.

messages.text: I have started a draft of the pricing and packaging model in A3 as part of T4, but I am not fully confident about the tiers and margin assumptions yet. Currently I am thinking of three tiers: a basic one off assessment, a standard package with a follow up session, and a premium option with a short series of check ins. I have used some rough estimates for time spent and internal costs, but I would appreciate your input on whether the structure makes sense and how we should position each tier commercially. Also, we need to think about any introductory discounts for the pilot clients under T9

I have reviewed the cost assumptions in A3. The three tier structure makes sense, but I think we should be more explicit about the time required for data preparation and quality checks, especially given the criteria we set in A2. Right now, the basic tier might be underestimating the effort. I suggest we add at least one extra hour for data validation in each tier and adjust the internal cost accordingly. That will help ensure that the margins we show in A3 are realistic before we take the proposal to senior management for approval

From the BI side, the main cost driver will be the time spent configuring and reviewing the dashboards defined in T3. For the basic tier, we can probably rely on a standard dashboard template with minimal customisation, which keeps the effort low. For the premium tier, if we include more tailored views or additional follow up analysis, we should reflect that in A3 as extra hours. I would also suggest that we limit the number of follow up sessions in the premium package to avoid open ended commitments that are hard to scale

From a market positioning perspective, three tiers are a good idea, but we should make sure each has a clear story. I would frame them roughly as: a quick financial health check, a deeper insight package with an action plan, and an ongoing guidance option. In A3, we can map these to specific inclusions so that later, when we work on A5 and A8, we can describe them consistently. On price points, we should aim for a clear step up between tiers, not just small increments, so that clients see a real difference in value

For PR and reputation, it is important that the pricing feels transparent and fair. I would avoid any complex add on fees in the first launch. Instead, we can define clear inclusions per tier in A3 and mention that any additional work beyond the scope will be quoted separately. For introductory discounts, I suggest we keep them limited to the pilot clients under T9 and frame them as a one time launch offer in our communications. That will help us avoid setting expectations for permanent discounts

Good point on the data validation time. I had not fully factored in the checks from A2. I will update A3 to add at least one extra hour per tier for that work and adjust the internal cost estimates. I might need your help to sanity check the resulting margins, as I am not entirely sure what target margin we should aim for on this service

I can help with that. As a starting point, we could aim for a margin that is at least in line with our other advisory services. Without sharing internal benchmarks here, I suggest we run a quick sensitivity check in A3: one scenario with conservative time estimates and one with slightly higher effort. If the margins are still acceptable in both, we can be more confident when we present T4 to senior management for approval

On the follow up sessions, I recommend we cap the premium tier at, say, three follow up calls within a defined period, for example three months. That keeps the effort predictable and easier to schedule. We can also specify in A3 that any additional sessions beyond that are billed separately. This will help us avoid overcommitting resources, especially if the service scales after the pilot

To make the tiers easy to communicate, I will later translate the inclusions from A3 into simple labels and one line descriptions in A5 and A8. For now, could we agree that the basic tier includes one assessment and one feedback session, the standard tier adds a more detailed action plan, and the premium tier adds the series of follow ups that 89373 mentioned If we lock that structure, I can start drafting messaging and internal enablement without waiting for the final price points

On introductory discounts, I propose we keep it simple: pilot clients under T9 receive a fixed percentage discount on the standard tier price, and we do not discount the basic tier further. That way, we encourage uptake of the more complete package without devaluing the entry level offer. We should also set a clear end date for the discount, aligned with the pilot timeline, and capture that in A3 and in the PR plan under T6

I am comfortable with that structure: basic equals one assessment plus one feedback session, standard adds a more detailed action plan, and premium adds up to three follow up calls within three months. I will update A3 to reflect these inclusions clearly for each tier. Once I have done that and adjusted the time estimates, I will share the updated model so we can agree on the final price points and margins before taking it to senior management as part of T4

Once you update A3, I will run through the numbers and confirm that the margins are acceptable for each tier, including the impact of the pilot discount that 509812 suggested. If everything looks reasonable, we can treat the tier structure and price ranges as final for the initial launch and prepare the summary needed for senior management approval under T4

On the pilot discount, aligning it with the standard tier and the T9 timeline works well from an operational standpoint. It will also give us a consistent data set to analyse in A7 and T12, since most pilot clients will be on the same package. We should just make sure that the discount is clearly flagged in A3 so that we do not accidentally treat it as the regular price later

Once the final price points are in A3, I will craft the value messaging for each tier in A5 and ensure that the internal deck in A8 and T10 explains the differences clearly. For the introductory discount, I will coordinate with 509812 so that the way we talk about it in marketing materials matches the PR narrative and does not create confusion about long term pricing

To close this out, I suggest we formally agree that the three tier structure and inclusions in A3 will be our final model for the initial launch, subject only to senior management sign off on the exact price points. We also agree that the pilot discount applies to the standard tier only, for a limited period aligned with T9. If everyone is aligned, we can record these as our decisions and move on to preparing the approval pack and external messaging

Agreed from my side. I will finalise A3 with the three tiers and inclusions we discussed and clearly mark the pilot discount conditions. Then I will prepare a short summary for senior management as part of T4, highlighting the structure, indicative margins, and the temporary nature of the pilot discount under T9

threads.thread_goal: Align marketing and PR messaging and lock the launch plan.

messages.text: I have drafted initial core marketing messages and a simple messaging matrix in A5 as part of T5, based on the scope in A1 and the tiered offer in A3. In parallel, 509812 has started outlining the PR launch plan under T6. Before we move too far, I would like us to align on the key messages, taglines, and the proposed launch date. The current draft positions the service around helping SME owners see, understand, and act on their numbers, with three tiers mapped to different needs. Could you review A5 and the PR outline and share any concerns, especially around regulatory language and the feasibility of the proposed launch timeline

Building on A5, I have drafted a PR plan under T6 that includes a press release, a small media briefing, and some thought leadership content over the following weeks. The plan assumes a launch date three weeks from now, which gives us time for legal review and for internal enablement via A8 and T10. The key messages mirror yours: clarity on financial health, simple insights, and practical next steps, without promising specific financial outcomes. I would like to confirm that this timing works for everyone and that we are comfortable with the level of external visibility in the first wave

I have read through A5 and the draft PR outline. The overall story feels aligned with the service concept in A1 and the tiers in A3. My only concern is whether we might be using language that sounds too close to investment advice in some parts. I am not fully sure where the line is, so I would prefer that legal reviews the key claims before we finalise. On timing, three weeks seems tight but doable from my side, as long as we can complete the playbook in A6 and the internal enablement in A8 in time

From a financial and compliance angle, I agree we should be careful not to imply guarantees or personalised investment advice. In A5, I noticed a few phrases that could be interpreted as promising improved profitability. I suggest we rephrase those to focus on helping clients understand their situation and explore options. Also, we should ensure that any references to data use are consistent with A4 and the consent requirements we are defining in T8. Once we have a near final version, I recommend a formal legal review before we lock the messaging and PR plan

From the BI side, the messages in A5 are consistent with what we can actually deliver with the dashboards defined in T3, as long as we avoid overpromising predictive capabilities. I would keep the language around trends and early warning signals, but avoid any suggestion that we can forecast exact outcomes. On the launch date, three weeks should be enough to finalise the core dashboards and test them with a small internal group, provided we keep scope stable

Good catch on the profitability language. I will go through A5 and replace any outcome oriented claims with wording that emphasises better understanding and informed decisions. I will also cross check with A4 to ensure that any mention of data use and privacy is aligned with the guidelines you are drafting in T8. Once I have a cleaned up version, we can send it to legal together with the PR materials from T6 for a combined review

On the investment advice concern, I share your view. In the PR materials under T6, I have already avoided any language that could be interpreted as promising returns, but I will double check once 21210 updates A5. For the launch date, three weeks gives us a bit of buffer before the 30 day deadline, which is useful in case legal feedback requires changes. If we all agree, I would like to tentatively lock that date, subject to final confirmation after legal review

Tentatively locking the launch date works for me, as long as we keep an eye on the readiness of A6 and A8. I will focus on getting the operational playbook in A6 to a solid draft in the next few days so that sales and support can be trained using A8 and T10 before we go live. If legal feedback forces major changes to the service description, we might need to adjust the playbook, but hopefully the core flow will remain stable

From my side, I will make sure that the dashboards and reporting views under T3 are ready for internal testing at least a week before the launch date. That will give us time to adjust any labels or visual elements that need to match the final wording in A5 and A8. If the messaging changes significantly after legal review, we will need to update some chart titles and explanations, but that should be manageable within the timeline

I have now updated A5 with the more cautious language we discussed and aligned the data use references with A4. The messaging matrix includes core messages, proof points, and do not say items to avoid regulatory issues. I propose that we treat this version as our candidate for final approval and send it, together with the PR plan and draft press release from T6, to legal for review. Assuming we get only minor comments, we can then formally approve A5 as the final messaging set for all external channels

I have reviewed the updated A5 and it looks consistent with the PR materials. The do not say section is particularly helpful for media interactions. Once legal signs off, I suggest we formally approve A5 as the single source of truth for external messaging and use it to update all channels under T11. That includes the website, sales collateral, and any social or content pieces we plan to run around launch

From my review, the updated A5 no longer contains any statements that look like guaranteed financial outcomes, and the references to data use are in line with the current draft of A4. I am comfortable recommending this version to legal for final review. Once they confirm, we can consider the messaging matrix approved and focus on executing the launch plan under T6 and T11

On the launch date, I have checked the PR plan and internal dependencies. If we assume legal feedback within a week, we can comfortably keep the launch three weeks from now. I propose we now confirm this date as our official target, again subject to any unforeseen regulatory blockers. This will allow us to lock media invitations, internal training sessions based on A8 and T10, and the final readiness checklist two days before go live

Assuming legal sign off, I am in favour of formally approving A5 as the final messaging matrix for all external channels. It will make T5, T10, and T11 much smoother if everyone refers to the same document. I will coordinate with channel owners to ensure that any existing materials are updated or replaced before launch, using A5 as the reference

I am aligned with confirming the launch date three weeks from now, provided legal does not raise any major red flags. This gives us a clear target for finalising A6 and running the internal enablement sessions based on A8 and T10. I will plan the playbook walkthrough accordingly and coordinate with sales and support so they are ready before go live

With these confirmations, I will proceed on the basis that D7 and D8 are agreed: A5 becomes the approved messaging matrix for all external channels once legal signs off, and the launch date is set for three weeks from now, barring any regulatory blockers. I will update the PR plan under T6 accordingly and start locking media activities and spokesperson availability

threads.thread_goal: Review pilot results and agree on improvements before broader rollout.

messages.text: We have now completed the initial pilot with a small group of SME clients, and I have summarised the results and feedback in A7 as part of T12. Overall, clients appreciated the clarity of the dashboards and the structured conversations, but we saw some friction around data preparation and the amount of information in the reports. I would like us to review the key findings and agree on a short list of improvements to the service, the playbook in A6, and the materials in A8 before we scale beyond the pilot. Please take a look at A7 and share your top two or three changes you think we should prioritise

Looking at A7, one theme I noticed is that some clients felt overwhelmed by the amount of detail in the first session. In A6, the playbook currently suggests going through all KPIs in one go, which might be too much. I would propose we adjust T7 so that consultants focus on a smaller set of priority metrics in the first meeting and leave the rest for follow up. Also, a few clients mentioned that the action points were not always clear enough, so we might need to simplify the way we capture recommendations in the report template

From my review of A7, the biggest pain point seems to be data preparation. Several clients struggled to provide clean data that met the A2 criteria, and consultants spent extra time fixing issues. For the next wave, I suggest we strengthen the pre engagement checklist in A2 and A8, and perhaps add a short pre call step in A6 where we verify data quality before scheduling the main session. This might add a bit of time upfront but should reduce surprises during the assessment

On the communication side, A7 shows that some clients were not fully clear on what to expect from the sessions, especially regarding the level of detail and the follow up. For the broader rollout, I recommend we refine the client facing description in A8 and the sales scripts under T10 to set clearer expectations: what happens before, during, and after the assessment. We might also add a simple one page overview that consultants can send ahead of time, summarising the process and what the client needs to prepare

From a reputation perspective, the pilot feedback in A7 is encouraging, but we should address the points about complexity and data friction before we amplify the service in PR. I agree with simplifying the first session and clarifying expectations. Additionally, we might want to collect a couple of short client quotes, with consent, that highlight the benefits in simple language. These can be used in future PR and marketing materials, as long as they stay within the boundaries of A5 and A4

I agree that data preparation is a key area to improve. For the dashboards, we can add a simple pre check view that highlights missing or inconsistent data before the main analysis. In A6, we can insert a step where the consultant reviews this pre check and either proceeds or asks the client to correct issues. I will also work with 21210 to ensure that the readiness section in A8 and T10 reflects these expectations more clearly, so clients know what is needed before they sign up

On simplifying the first session, I can adjust T7 so that the playbook suggests focusing on three to five key metrics that matter most for the clients situation, rather than going through the full list. I might need some help identifying which metrics should be the default starting point, but we can at least change the flow so that consultants are encouraged to prioritise. We can also add a template section in A6 for a short, plain language summary of the top three insights and actions

To make the pre engagement checklist more effective, I will update A2 and coordinate with 21210 so that the simplified version in A8 and T10 uses client friendly language. For example, instead of listing specific accounting terms, we can ask for last 12 months of income and expense records in digital form. This should reduce confusion and help clients prepare the right files before the assessment

I will take the lead on refining A8 and the sales scripts under T10 based on the pilot insights in A7. Specifically, I will add a simple journey view: what happens before, during, and after the session, and what the client needs to do at each step. I will also work with 8267 to ensure that the way we describe the session flow matches the updated playbook in A6 and T7, so that there is no disconnect between what we promise and what actually happens

On client quotes, I can draft a short consent form and a simple template for capturing testimonials that stay within the boundaries of A5 and A4. We should be careful not to highlight any individual financial outcomes, but we can safely use comments about clarity, confidence, and understanding. Once we have a couple of strong quotes, we can incorporate them into future PR activities and, where appropriate, into A8

For the default starting metrics, I suggest we focus on revenue trend, gross margin, operating cash flow, and a simple liquidity indicator. These are already in the dashboards and are easy to explain. I will update the dashboard views so that these metrics appear first, and we can reflect that order in A6 and T7. That should help consultants guide the conversation more naturally and avoid overwhelming clients with too many numbers at once

That list of starting metrics is helpful. I will incorporate it into the playbook steps in A6 and T7, so that consultants know where to begin.
